newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: First Moslems in dock in Bosnia war crimes trial.
newsitem.headline: First Moslems in dock in Bosnia war crimes trial.

text.p: The first trial of Moslems accused of atrocities against Bosnian Serbs began on Monday before the U.N. tribunal charged with trying war crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia.
The trial of three Moslems and a Croat, is a watershed for the international tribunal, which has faced accusations from Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serbs of anti-Serb bias.

The trial, the third hearing on alleged war crimes in Bosnia, involves the highest-ranking defendants tried to date, and marks the first time suspects have been handed over to The Hague by their native countries.
It is also the tribunal's first group trial.
Moslems Hazim Delic, Esad Landzo and Zejnil Delalic and Croat Zdravko Mucic are accused of war crimes against Serbs at the Celebici camp, near Konjic in central Bosnia during 1992.
Mucic, the 41-year-old former camp commander, and Delalic, 48 and a former Bosnian Moslem regional military leader, are accused of command responsibility for atrocities at the camp.
They are charged with at least 14 murders and with a grim catalogue of torture, rape and sexual assault.
Deputy camp commander Delic, 32, is also charged with command responsibility and, along with 23-year-old camp guard Landzo, of taking part in torture, rapes and killings.

Delic and Landzo are accused of beating men to death with wooden planks, baseball bats, shovels and lengths of cable and of torturing detainees, many aged over 60, with pliers, acid, electric shock and hot metal pincers.
One detainee was said to have had a Moslem political badge nailed to his forehead.

Delic and Landzo were arrested in Bosnia last May and handed over to the tribunal, the first time the authorities in any of the former Yugoslav republics had exercised an arrest warrant issued by the warcrimes body.
Mucic was detained in Vienna and Delalic in Munich a year ago. All four have claimed their innocence.

The tribunal, set up by the U.N. Security Council in 1993, has faced accusations from Pale and Belgrade of anti-Serb bias, but has repeatedly stated that its war crimes investigations are carried out irrespective of political or ethnic background.
Most of the 74 men charged are Serbs but only seven suspects are in the tribunal's custody.

Tribunal judges are expected later this month to announce their verdict in the six-month trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic, accused of killing, raping and torturing Moslems in northwest Bosnia in 1992.
Last November Croat Drazen Erdemovic was handed a 10-year jail sentence after pleading guilty to taking part in a Serb massacre of over 1,200 unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
He is appealing against the sentence.
